channel.title: Inkisle Journal
channel.description: The making of Inkisle, one post a day: design decisions, prototypes, mistakes and numbers.

item.title: Keeping two devices in step: moving iCloud sync into a shared app kit
item.description: Inkisle's progress, ink and settings were already matched across devices through iCloud. On November 16 we moved that bridge into a shared app kit. How we kept saved data intact, the merge rules that never shrink, how the purchase mark is handled, and what we have not checked on real devices.

item.title: An ending that plays once, and a lighthouse to see it again
item.description: The season 1 ending of Inkisle plays by itself exactly once, the first time the last stage of act 30 is cleared. How we set the replay rules, how players who already cleared it and the act 10 ending are handled, and what we have not checked on translations or a real device.

item.title: Skip a stage after three losses: a gentle offer with a cost
item.description: In Inkisle, losing the same stage three times offers to skip it for 3 Ink. How the offer is timed, which stages are excluded, how a skipped stage shows on the chart, and how it is saved.

item.title: Release notes inside the app: a 12-language sheet and a length check
item.description: Inkisle's release notes are a sheet inside Settings, not a web page. How each build's notes are written in 12 languages, the checks on item count and length, and the test bug that showed an empty sheet.

item.title: Two free seas and one unlock: how we simplified payment
item.description: Inkisle keeps seas 1 and 2 free and opens the rest with one purchase, Unlock All Seas. How consumable ink is set up, how the lock is computed in code, the lines we drew on restore and refunds, and what we have not tested.

item.title: From 100 acts to 30, and an ending that stays open: the end of season 1
item.description: The first plan was 100 acts and 800 stages. Why we closed season 1 at 30 acts and 240 stages, how we kept the 100-act plan as a candidate instead of dropping it, and how the ending with no closing word was made.

item.title: Bots as playtesters: a warning that rarely cries wolf
item.description: A crisis warning should only appear when you are really about to lose. We replayed thousands of bot games to measure false alarms, and the same run showed a star goal almost nobody wins.

item.title: One shape and one color per sea: how the chart marks what you cleared
item.description: On the sea chart, stages you have not cleared stay white everywhere, and cleared ones take the shape and color of their sea. The rule, the fourteen styles, the contrast check and how we looked at a wide screen.

item.title: Two tests that lied: a screen size and a language that leaked
item.description: Phone-sized tests quietly ran with a tablet-sized screen, and two tests left the language setting behind for the next ones. How both showed up and what fixed them, with no change to the app itself.

item.title: Not a stretched phone: giving Inkisle its own iPad layout
item.description: On an iPad the battle screen used to be the phone screen made bigger. How the board got side panels in landscape, why a 9.7-inch iPad needed narrower ones, and what we have and have not checked.

item.title: Two Ink items at once: slots, gaps and what the bots told us
item.description: In early seas you could run one Ink item at a time. From sea 5 you can run two, and later three, with a gap between starts. The rule table, how the button shows it, and a simulation that found a much smaller effect than we expected.

item.title: A sea chart that changes its road: one line style per sea
item.description: With 14 seas on one scrolling chart, the road between stages looked the same everywhere. We gave each sea its own line style, color and wiggle, made the angle continue across sea borders, and only draw what is on screen. The values, the tests, and what we have not seen on a phone.

item.title: A difficulty curve with a floor: no stage the simplest bot can never win
item.description: With hundreds of stages, a few hard ones are not a few hard ones, they are a wall. We retuned all 14 seas to a curve with a rest stage in every sea, capped how strong the enemy AI may be, and added a test that fails if the simplest bot wins 0 of 40. The before and after.

item.title: The white sea's ink spring: when a three-star rule cannot be earned
item.description: Sea 14 has a spring that spreads ink onto nearby islands. Bots could not earn the three-star goal "make the spring spread to N islands", so we measured, tried moving islands, and replaced the rule with a count of spring pulses. What we tried and what is still unchecked.

item.title: What the app does not have: no ads, no accounts, no tracking
item.description: Some of Inkisle's design is about what is left out. The app asks for no account and has no ads or tracking tools, it runs on iOS and Android from one codebase, and we drew a new icon for both. What we decided and what we have not checked.

item.title: When saved data breaks: how the app recovers
item.description: A phone can lose, truncate or block an app's saved data. How Inkisle handles missing, damaged, outdated and unavailable storage for progress, the intro and the sound setting, and where our recovery is still blunt.

item.title: Three stars, one rule: how a stage is rated
item.description: Every stage in Inkisle can earn up to three stars. What each star means, why stars never block progress or go down, the 13 kinds of three-star goals, and the wrong label we found and fixed.

item.title: A drag that forgives: the small rules behind one gesture
item.description: Sending a fleet in Inkisle is one drag. The small rules that make it work with a real finger: a wider pick area, a drag that samples the whole path, one finger at a time, and clear messages when a send is not possible.

item.title: Sound that is off by default: a scale for each sea
item.description: Inkisle starts silent and the player turns sound on. How the sounds are made in code with no audio files, how each sea gets its own five-note scale, and why a chain of captures climbs the scale.

item.title: Ink that spreads: the small effects that say what just happened
item.description: In Inkisle a captured island leaves a bloom of ink, a comeback shows a banner, and the last enemy island lights up. What each effect is for, how long it lasts, and how the first-run finger hint works.

item.title: A ten-second intro in three versions: sky, sea and land
item.description: Inkisle opens with a ten-second intro that comes in three versions. How the three share one ending, why a shuffled bag decides which one you see, when it shortens to three seconds, and what happens with reduce-motion turned on.

item.title: Sending from several islands at once: three rewrites of one control
item.description: Attacking one island from several of yours was the hardest control in Inkisle. The first drag-based version, the tap-to-select fix and the swipe-to-select version, and what each one taught us.

item.title: Tuning difficulty with bots: five stages that were wrong
item.description: We played every stage with simple bots for 40 seeds each and found stages that were impossible, too short or too hard. The five changes, the win rates before and after, and why bots are not people.

item.title: A playable prototype in a day
item.description: Sixteen stages, two seas and one HTML file of about 95 KB with no outside requests. How the prototype is built, what we tested in a headless browser, and what we could not test.

item.title: Art direction: three mockups, one pick
item.description: We asked for the same battle screen from our design assistant (two directions) and from GPT. What each returned, what went wrong with the outside mockup, and why minimal vector won.

item.title: Naming the game: how we ended up with Inkisle
item.description: Ten English name candidates, five finalists, a store and domain check, and why Inkisle won. Including the weak spots we know about and the checks we have not done.

item.title: The rules on one page: islands, troops, capture
item.description: Inkisle's whole rule set on one page: how islands produce troops, how fleets fly, how capture is calculated, and how a match ends. Starting values, before testing.

item.title: Four game ideas, one core: why we chose island conquest
item.description: We drafted four concepts for our next game. All four shared one core, sending troops between nodes. Here is why we kept the core, dropped the story and put it on the sea.
